articles.title: How an ad gets its message across

body.support:
An ad is a **film text**. It has a **purpose**. Maybe to sell. Maybe to warn. It is made for an **audience**.

Everything in it is chosen.

1. **Pictures.** A **close-up** shows a face. A **wide shot** shows the place.
2. **Sound.** Music tells you how to feel.
3. **Words.** Words on screen. A **call to action** tells you what to do.
4. **Shape.** A **hook** to grab you. Then the **message**. Then the call to action.

An ad for teens might be funny and fast. An ad for older people might be slow and calm.

Ask: **What is it for? Who is it for? How do the pictures, sound and words help?**
body.core:
An ad is a **film text** with a clear **purpose** — to sell, to warn, to change what you do — and a clear **audience**. Everything in it is a choice.

1. **Pictures.** A **close-up** shows a face and a feeling. A **wide shot** shows the place. Bright colours feel fun; dark colours feel serious.
2. **Sound.** Music tells you how to feel. A voice-over explains. A sudden sound effect makes you jump.
3. **Words.** Text on screen, a catchy **slogan**, and a **call to action**: the thing they want you to do.
4. **Structure.** Most ads follow a shape: a **hook** in the first few seconds, a **build**, the **message**, then the **call to action**.

The makers think hard about the audience. An ad for teens might use humour, music and fast cuts. An ad for older people might be slower and calmer.

To pull an ad apart, ask: **What's it for? Who's it for? How do the pictures, sound and words help?**
body.extend:
An advertisement is a **film text** constructed for a specific **purpose** — to sell, to warn, to change behaviour — and a specific **audience**. Nothing in it is accidental.

1. **Visuals.** Shot types position the viewer: a **close-up** builds emotion, a **wide shot** establishes setting. Colour, lighting and editing pace set the **tone**.
2. **Sound.** Music cues emotion, voice-over explains, and sound effects create surprise or tension.
3. **Language.** On-screen text, a memorable **slogan**, and a **call to action** that tells the audience what to do.
4. **Structure.** Most ads hook the viewer in the first few seconds, build interest, deliver the message, then close with the call to action.

These choices depend on the audience. A campaign aimed at teenagers might use humour, music and rapid editing; one for older viewers might be slower and more direct.

To analyse an ad, ask: **What is its purpose? Who is the audience? How do visuals, sound, language and structure work together?**

caseStudies.title: Dumb Ways to Die

body.support:
In **2012**, **Metro Trains Melbourne** made a safety ad. It did not look like a safety ad.

It was a cartoon song called **Dumb Ways to Die**. Cute characters died in silly ways. The song was catchy.

At the end came the real message: be safe around **trains**.

People all over the world shared it, because it was funny. In 2013 it won big awards for ads.

The makers knew their audience. Young people often ignore serious safety ads. So they hid the message in something fun.
body.core:
In **November 2012**, **Metro Trains Melbourne** released a safety campaign made by the ad agency **McCann Melbourne**. It didn't look like a safety ad at all.

It was a cartoon music video called **Dumb Ways to Die**. Cute, colourful characters met silly ends to a catchy song. Only near the end did the real message arrive: some of the dumbest ways to die are around trains. Then came the call to action: **be safe around trains**.

It spread around the world online, and people shared it because it was funny, not because it was a warning. In 2013 it won **five Grand Prix awards** at the Cannes Lions, one of the world's biggest advertising festivals.

The makers knew their audience: young people who tune out serious safety messages. So they hid the message inside something people *wanted* to watch.
body.extend:
In **November 2012**, **Metro Trains Melbourne** launched a rail safety campaign made by the agency **McCann Melbourne**. It took an unexpected approach. Instead of scary warnings, it was a cartoon music video: **Dumb Ways to Die**.

Colourful characters met absurd ends to a cheerful, catchy song. Only towards the end did the real subject appear — dangerous behaviour around trains — followed by the call to action: **be safe around trains**.

The video spread internationally because audiences enjoyed it and chose to share it. In 2013 it won **five Grand Prix awards** at the Cannes Lions, a major world advertising festival.

It was made for young people, who often ignore serious safety ads. By hiding the warning inside something fun, the makers turned viewers into people who spread the message.

source.name: Campaign Brief — “Australian Campaigns of the Decade: Metro Trains ‘Dumb Ways to Die’ (2012) via McCann Melbourne”; Mumbrella (Cannes Lions 2013)

teacher.overview: Students analyse how a film text (an ad) uses pictures, sound, words and structure to reach a specific audience for a specific purpose, using Metro Trains Melbourne's “Dumb Ways to Die”. They then plan, storyboard and film (or perform) their own 30-second safety ad for people their age and test whether the message landed.
prep: Queue the official Dumb Ways to Die video (Metro Trains Melbourne's YouTube channel) and preview it. It's a cartoon, but it's about deaths: check it suits your students.
Have a few other short ads ready for comparison.
Check your school's rules on filming and sharing student videos; acting live is a fine alternative.

**Ad plan:** 1 purpose; 2 audience; 3 hook (first 3 seconds); 4 sound (music then silence); 5 slogan / words on screen; 6 call to action.

**Pull apart (sample):** audience — young people around trains; hook — catchy song and cute characters; pictures — bright colours, simple cartoon; sound — cheerful, catchy song; call to action — be safe around trains.

**Case study:** Metro Trains Melbourne, made by McCann Melbourne, released November 2012; purpose: rail safety; funny because young audiences tune out serious warnings; message at the end so people watch it all.
